utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Kovacic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Akhavan. I'm Bozidar Kovacic, and with my colleague Mikulicic, I present the defence of Mr. Mario Cerkez. I shall ask my questions in Croatian, and will you, please, between you hearing the end of the question and your answer, make a short break just for the interpretation's sake, and if there's anything that you do not understand about my questions, please draw my attention to it. During your testimony in chief, you said that at some point you also visited Mr. Cerkez too. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was, if I understood you properly, after your visit with Mr. Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I am correct, it was on the 4th of May, sometime around 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was on the first floor of a building called the cinema hall or the Workers' University? I don't know if you've heard that term.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the cinema.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it could be about 150 metres away from the hotel where you had your meeting with Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember but it sounds reasonable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you can't remember because the whole situation was very confused; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I just don't remember what the proximity of the two buildings was, but obviously they were very close with each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you agree that they were very close?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the meeting with Cerkez were you explained his function, his duties, and who was it that gave you that explanation?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was told that Mr. Cerkez was the commander of HVO forces in Vitez. I don't recall exactly who told me that but it would have been a member of the British Battalion. I believe, from my notes, I may even have been told about -- yes. On the first page of my handwritten notes. In the first day of the briefing you can see the reference to Commander Mario Cerkez, and I was probably told before the meeting sometime as well the same information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct. Quite correct. And since you are referring to your notes and since you looked up the first page of your notes, would it then be correct to say that these notes, and I believe you just said that but I simply want to make sure, is it then correct to say that the notes on the first page is what you were told by others after you arrived in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Before I had a chance to verify certain matters with Mr. Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It means it was part of that briefing that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Sefkija Dzidic was mentioned then?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm trying to see what -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page one?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The top of the page, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was also referred to as the commander of the local defence?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was also mention of Mensur Klestura also as a commander, evidently on the Muslim side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And above Klestura's name, "325th Brigade of the BH army"?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Evidently with his headquarters at Preocica and here it is somehow related to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the second part below now concerns the other side, the HVO?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here we have mention of Tihomir Blaskic, and with him you met subsequently and you ascertained that he was not the commander. Will you please say "Yes" or "No" because of the record?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also told that the commander of the Vitez HVO, and if I understand your notes, you put in brackets "(town defence)"?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that that person was Mario Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then your note goes on about the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade as a joint Novi Travnik-Vitez Brigade, the commander of which was Mario Cerkez? First page. We're still on page 1.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you have a note, a remark reading more or less, it seems, that the joint Novi Travnik-Vitez Brigade is about to become an autonomous brigade?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of some documents and reports of the British Battalion, did they tell you how positive were they, how sure were they that that brigade -- or let me try to be more accurate. What progress has been made towards that transformation of the brigade? Did they tell you that? How far had they got with their transforming the brigade?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: All I can recall is what I have in my notes really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it jog your memory if I said that perhaps the name of the brigade was mentioned during that briefing, that is, as the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. In response to your answer, I do recall from my meeting with Mr. Cerkez that he referred to himself as the commander of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever, during those interviews or in any other way, that is, on the basis of documents, from documents, have you ever established the meaning of that brigade name, the Vitez Brigade? What does it mean, that name?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: If you are referring to the area of command, I believe it's dealt with, according to my notes once again, the control of Vitez town and surrounding villages. This, once again, is based on my meeting with Mr. Cerkez, on page 32 of my handwritten notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But would you agree with me or disagree with me if I said that this particular name of the brigade, in the Croatian language, is an adjective, and it is indicative of the origin of the brigade, where it comes from?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm really not in a position to comment on that. I can only refer back to what I was told by Mr. Cerkez and the British Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you asked no particular questions about that, did you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: About the meaning of the name of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on, but I'm still with your notes. So Mr. Pero Skopljak was mentioned to you as the commander of the town defence?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the same individual's name comes up again on page 24 of your notes. I believe that the pages are not marked identically. So just to see where we are, it's the page which begins, it says, "Deputy" something in the upper left corner. Here I see the names of Nenad Santic, Zarko Kristo, and then we again see Pero Skopljak, but now Pero Skopljak, and in brackets -- no, sorry, below that, so beneath the name of Skopljak, there is again a comment, "Leader of the HVO municipality or the Vitez municipality"?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Pero Skopljak is again mentioned here as one of the HVO leaders associated with the area of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then on page 25, rather, the next page of your notes, we seem to have a structure or, rather, an organisational chart. I should like to ask you, this note, on page 25, are these conclusions that you drew after all those interviews that you had, where you're now trying to make a kind of a chart of that picture that was painted to you in various interviews, or is it the product of something that you were told by one person?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it would have been more than the product of what one person -- it would probably be the information which was gathered through speaking to several people, and as you see, the name of those in positions of leadership appear in various parts of my notes. So this is probably based on one meeting, but you will see similar charts or indications elsewhere. If I may just explain, I was interested not in gathering specific names for the report, because the report did not, as a rule, mention any names, nor was it mandated to look at particular individuals, but I wanted to know, generally speaking, who is who in the region and to try and understand the situation better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe it's quite logical, and that is what I would do if I were in your place. That is how I read this, that it was simply a note for you, that you just wanted to have a clear picture for yourself to know who is who. But what I should like to know, this seems to be a kind of chain of command or something here, although you, as investigator, were not particularly concerned with that. I mean, that was not your mission there. But, nevertheless, it seems to refer to a kind of hierarchy, even in relation to Ahmici. There is no brigade commander, the commander of the brigade, rather, that is headquartered in Vitez. That is not here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Not to have to go back to your notes, perhaps I might just, on page 32, here you were evidently making notes about interviewing Mr. Cerkez; is that so?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that this name in capital letters above the name is the duty, is that it, above the name?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall repeat. Here, in the upper half of the page, in your hand evidently, you wrote, "Commander of the Vitez Brigade."

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you added a name above it in capital letters, I presume, because it is so difficult to write our names, and somebody must have helped you because of the spelling, but I presume we are talking about the meeting with Cerkez. We agree with that, don't we?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you remember, of course, we know that six years have elapsed since, but would you remember who was present at that meeting, or shall I perhaps try to remind you? According to what you said and what we heard, you were there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then there was Cerkez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also Matthew Dundas-Whatley was there?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was Osorio, Thomas Osorio?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was not at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Thomas was not at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: And there was one of the -- a soldier who was with Mr. Cerkez who left after I requested that he leave the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was at the beginning of the meeting, so when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was also a soldier in Cerkez's office, and in your earlier testimony, I don't want really to go back to it, but you said, I believe you will agree, that he was kind of a glum type or gloomy type, that he had an Uzi, and that he was wearing a German uniform or rather a uniform with German insignia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that it was a German soldier?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would doubt that it was a German soldier. I know that there were a lot of surplus army uniforms which the locals wore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct, I don't want to waste too much time, but I believe in one of your two statements, I believe you said that that particular soldier was a mercenary, or perhaps I got things mixed up because you have been testifying for quite some time now. Yes, quite. That was what you told the investigators on the 25th of June, 1995. Let me rephrase the question. I understand that he looked, to you, like a mercenary, that is, his appearance. I do not think that you are claiming here that he was a mercenary; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I did not inquire who he was, but he did not appear to be a regular soldier because of his uniform and also because of the weapon that he had and his general demeanour, but I did not inquire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From this whole team which was there, did it never occur to you that he might be a security officer?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: He could have been, but there were others in the building who appeared to be regular HVO soldiers who were probably security officers. I'm not sure what he was doing there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. It doesn't really matter. But whatever the case, you asked Cerkez to send him away because you did not feel comfortable in his presence, and Cerkez told him to leave the room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He was pointing his machine gun at me, so I suggested that we could have a better conversation without him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Incidentally, you also had some security officers with you, weren't there? There were three of them escorting you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe it was only Dundas-Whatley in the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not remember that there were three British soldiers with big weapons who stayed in front of the door, behind the door of the office?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps they stayed down there in the hall. Perhaps I had the wrong information.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Usually from what I recall, the British Battalion would deliver me to the door of the building and I would only go into the office with Dundas-Whatley. The other soldiers would usually stay at the entrance of the building and not come to the meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you are not quite sure if they were or if they were not, if I'm reading this properly?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't say with certainty, but I don't believe that that would have been the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, be that as it may, during the interview there were no security officers in the room. In the room there were present only those people that we mentioned awhile ago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Cerkez was quite willing to talk to you and that he was cooperative?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. On the whole, I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it then correct that sometime in the course of that meeting, sometime halfway through that meeting, you were also joined by the commander of the BritBat, General Robert Stewart?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct. Colonel. When Stewart arrived, could you, as an observer -- did you think that Stewart and Cerkez knew one another already and they were talking to one another as fellow soldiers, as colleagues?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. They would seem to have known each other quite well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that also hold true of Matthew Dundas-Whatley?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall. I suppose they knew each other. It didn't really leave any impression on me. But when Bob Stewart entered the room, I believe that his relationship with Mario Cerkez suggested that they knew each other well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you began your meeting -- and it was roughly along these lines so will you please only confirm "Yes" or "No"? Of course, this is very tentative, because I'm trying to cut it short. Oh, by the way, did you ask for permission to tape the interview, to tape the conversation?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were not taping that conversation, were you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you know if anyone else was recording that conversation?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember anyone recording the meeting, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And nobody said that it was being recorded?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Nobody said, but it's possible that it could have been recorded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it more or less go along these lines -- I really don't want to go into details -- first you asked some questions about the task, about the terms of reference of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You asked Cerkez to confirm that he was indeed the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then Cerkez explained it to you, that it was a recently-founded brigade, that it had not been properly organised yet, and that it was still being structured and organised; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall him telling me that, meaning to say I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Quite. Never mind. This was, anyway, the introduction to the proper interview. You then asked him whether he knew what had happened in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I recall that most of the interview had focused on what had transpired in Vitez rather than Ahmici, on the assumption that the area of authority of Mr. Cerkez focused on Vitez, but I'm sure at some point Ahmici was mentioned as well, but it was not the focus of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that in that conversation he mentioned that according to information that he had received subsequently, that there were soldiers wearing black uniforms in parts of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The only reference I have in my notes to HOS, which I assume would be those who would be wearing black uniforms, is on page 33, towards the bottom, where Mr. Cerkez suggested that HOS was present during the hostilities in Vitez, that there were no HOS in Vitez but that they came from Zenica, that they were mixed Muslim and Croats. Again, towards the end of our meeting, we briefly discussed Ahmici, where he said that the HVO was not responsible and where he suggested that HOS was responsible. I don't recall him mentioning specifically that people were wearing black uniforms, he simply referred to HOS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of that page, since we're talking about it, you seem to have made a conclusion of your own there. First, you said HOS again, and a question mark. So you must have heard HOS mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean mentioned before in the same meeting? Yes. The reason I put the question mark was not because I did not know what HOS was but because I, in my own mind, questioned the explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the earlier meeting or at briefings with the British Battalion, did you hear mention of HOS?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: HOS did not figure prominently in my notes in terms of the briefings with the British Battalion. I do remember from my own memory that it was clearly mentioned on several occasions, and there is, I believe on page 5, I'm not sure if this is from my briefing from the British Battalion, towards the end of page 5: "There were HOS troops in that area at the time but no eyewitness accounts of their involvement."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: But I think the question was whether HOS had a very key role to play or a marginal role, and for that reason most of my discussions with the British Battalion focused on the HVO rather than HOS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sure we will agree. We're back to 33 now, and that is after the talk with Cerkez, you noted HOS and a question mark, which means that you still had a question in your mind. That is my conclusion. Would you agree with it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had a question in my mind whether it was credible to say that HOS was responsible for Ahmici or Vitez, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And below that you have written: "HVO did not do it." That is the conclusion from the meeting with Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. This is a description of what Mr. Cerkez was telling me. It is not my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. At a point during the meeting when Stewart was there, you discussed the list of perpetrators, alleged perpetrators; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean the list of 18 individuals which my colleague Thomas Osorio --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was probably discussed at some point. I recall it was discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then towards the end of the meeting, you had told Blaskic a little earlier, this time talking to Cerkez, you said that he should, that it is his duty, and apparently he was told this in the form of advice, that he should conduct an investigation. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This matter was discussed when Colonel Stewart arrived, and it was mentioned by myself but mainly by Colonel Stewart, and it was in the form of advice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to be quite sure, did that mean an investigation at the level of the brigade, as I would assume?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It meant an investigation with respect to the subordinates of Mr. Cerkez, whoever those happened to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was clearly implied, was it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that he was responsible for the actions of his subordinates, for those who were under his command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (In English) Right. So in other words, of his unit?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct. His unit or others over which he exercised authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we go on to another area now just to clear up a few points that have been discussed? One further point in connection with that interview, in your statement you said that Cerkez seemed concerned to you.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think he seemed concerned, especially when Colonel Stewart arrived and began speaking about how Cerkez bears a responsibility for ensuring that this matter is investigated and dealt with effectively. I think he visibly became nervous, and obviously the whole tempo of the meeting changed after Colonel Stewart arrived and after we began to discuss this issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cerkez asked that Colonel Stewart give him this list so that he might start the investigation, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The 4th of May, when I was meeting with Cerkez, the list of 18 individuals was not available yet. Actually, my colleague, Thomas Osorio, was in Zenica on the same day, interviewing some of the witnesses. So the list would not have been available at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you remember that Cerkez said to you, "Give me the names so that I can institute proceedings"?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't specifically remember that, but if you're referring in relation to the 18 names, that would not have been possible because there was no discussion of that. It may be that Mr. Cerkez would have said, "I don't remember," but it's plausible that he said, "Let me know if you come up with any evidence and I will look into it." But our standard explanation was that we were not there to investigate for the HVO or other authorities, that was their own responsibility, and there was no desire on our part to get into the business of criminal investigations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree with you that, at the time, Colonel Stewart didn't have this list of 18 names, as it was compiled later, but he did say during the meeting that they knew some names, and Cerkez said, "Well, give me the names, since you think that I should carry out an investigation, because this will be of assistance to me." Mr. Stewart refused for security reasons, because of the sources of information. Do you remember that? Have I reminded you of that?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember it, but it's possible that that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put it in a different way. The atmosphere at the meeting, was it a constructive atmosphere or a hostile atmosphere, and in view of the kind of atmosphere that prevailed, would you think that something like that may have been said?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: All I can tell you is that relative to my meetings with others, such as Dario Kordic and Colonel Blaskic, that the meeting with Cerkez was, by far, the best. I think the atmosphere was generally favourable, as much as it could be under the circumstances. I do believe, as I said, when Colonel Stewart arrived, that the level of tension or, if you like, the lack of ease, certainly on the part of Mr. Cerkez, increased visibly, but I don't think it was a hostile meeting. It was more a case of Mr. Cerkez being perhaps intimidated by what Colonel Stewart had to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me one more thing: When you were leaving that meeting with Matthew Dundas-Whatley, who was escorting you, did you perhaps exchange a few thoughts or comments or the feeling that you had, that you had acquired during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never mind. I apologise. During your examination-in-chief, on several occasions, you spoke about Ahmici and Vitez, the events in Ahmici and in Vitez, making some kind of a parallel comment, but according to what you said, it would appear that you focused on the investigation of the events in Ahmici. Would it be true to say that the events in Vitez itself were not in the focus of your attention?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I think that we looked at Vitez as well. We, I think, spent a considerable amount of time looking, for example, at the truck bomb that was used in the Muslim quarters of the city and other such incidents. But, yes, Ahmici, because it was so blatant and extreme, was of greater interest to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your talks about Vitez as well, did you gain an impression that Vitez was divided, first into two zones, one under the control of the BH army or, rather, the Territorial Defence, the part of the city known as Mahala in Stari Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the same time, that the Croats had control over the other part of the city?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. From what I recall, the Croats had control over most of the city, and the Muslims were in Mahala in Stari Vitez, which was more like a sort of a defensive enclave surrounded by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further on, in the course of your investigation, did you learn that various forces controlled various parts of the town, the part of the town that was under the overall control of the Croats, put it that way?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean to say that in the area that was under the overall control of Croats, that there were pockets controlled by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that there were pockets controlled by various Croatian units, within the Croatian part of the town, several different Croatian units.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean units belonging to different armed forces or different units of the same armed forces?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first, the former.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall that. The impression which I gathered was that the HVO/HDZ was very much in control, at least of the areas under Croat authority, and that the HOS and other paramilitaries were more like roaming bands, rather than armed forces which actually controlled a particular geographical area. That was what I was led to believe also in my discussions with the HVO military commanders, such as Mr. Blaskic and Cerkez and also with Mr. Dario Kordic, and most of them said that the HOS were not from Vitez at all, that they were from Zenica. They were not a sort of local presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It seems that there is no translation for the clients in Croatian, but I'm listening to the English in order to see when the witness finishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a problem apparently with the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is translation in Croatian now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's coming now. Let us know if there is a further problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, during your testimony, you said that when you were in Ahmici, you saw three local Croat soldiers looting in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say they were Croat soldiers. I've indicated earlier that, from the distance, it was difficult to identify them. All I can say is that they were wearing military uniforms, and from the fact that that area was under Croat control and they didn't seem to be operating under stealth or fear that they were going to be captured, I assumed that they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, would you agree with me, and you spent quite some time there, that a uniform was not a distinctive sign on the basis of which you could tell who belonged to whom, at least not a reliable sign?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's true. Military uniforms were readily available, and most, if not all, men of military age wore them. It would require being close enough to see the patch on the shoulder to determine whether they belonged to a particular army or not. That's why I've not said in this particular case that the soldiers in the village were necessarily HVO, for example, but I assumed that they belonged to the local Croat population. But then again, in view of the fact that there was virtually universal mobilisation of men of military age, most men of military age who wore uniforms did belong to the regular armed forces, if you like. That was the impression, in general, which we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One or the other armed forces, if I may say, that those soldiers belonged to one or other military force?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. In view of the fact that the paramilitary groups had relatively small numbers, in most cases, the men would be members of the HVO, as distinct from HOS or other irregular forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever, during your investigations, hear that Blaskic had issued an order to clear up the area, including the removal of bodies, to protection of what remained in the houses and the property? Did you ever hear about that?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall that, but it would surprise me because there really wasn't much left to protect, except the Croat homes and Croat inhabitants, which were maybe 20 per cent of the village's population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there were some houses that were partially damaged after all, so a part of the house could be used, and there were things inside, regardless of who they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not hear that such an order was issued, but it's possible that it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to our information, on the 27th of April, there was an important platoon of civil defence there who carried out the clearing up of the area, checking dead bodies, property, putting out fires, and so on. No one informed you about that?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No one informed me, and what we saw in the village didn't seem to suggest that that was the case. The British Battalion said that they had collected almost all of the bodies to take them to the morgue in Zenica, and we ourselves recall that clearly there were still bodies in the village. So it didn't seem as if much of a cleanup had been done when we arrived there on the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear that on the 28th of April, the bodies that were found in Ahmici were taken to Vitez to be buried? Because you only found some bodies. The casualties were higher, according to the information we have.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know the padre of the British Battalion did say that some bodies were buried in Vitez. It wasn't clear how many of those bodies were from Vitez, how many were from Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Never mind. That question has already been put to you. Mr. Akhavan, would you agree that the term "HVO," when you were talking to members of the British Battalion, that this was a general term used for a Croatian organisation or an organisation belonging to the Croats of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It referred, as far as I recall, to the Croatian Defence Council, which was a distinct army or armed forces and which was closely related to or virtually inseparable from the HDZ political party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you also learnt in Bosnia what the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was, the so-called HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you also learn that the HVO was the executive branch of authority of the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. In theoretical terms, our impression was that the distinction between the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the HDZ, and the HVO were quite blurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you manage, from any sources, to learn that the HVO, as the executive branch of government, consists of two components, the military and the civilian, regardless of the purity of that or the perfection or imperfection of such a division?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. We were told that there was a military and civilian component.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, this list of 18 names that you mentioned, do you know where that list ended up in the end?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The list was given to the commission of experts established by Security Council Resolution 780 in Geneva. We did not give the list to anybody because as I explained earlier, we believed it would be beyond our mandate to do so, and we may even have been reprimanded by the Special Rapporteur for engaging in investigations which didn't specifically concern our mandate. So we, as a courtesy, took down the names and statements and give them to the commission of experts, and at that point we were no longer involved in that specific question of how the commission chose to use the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But while you were there on the ground, you certainly didn't give it to the British Battalion as a return information to the briefing that they gave you at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't believe so, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that it was highly sensitive, as you said, so you felt that you could only give it upwards in the hierarchy to the superiors. That is how I understand what you are saying, that you didn't give it to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: My colleague, Thomas Osorio, would know best how the information was used, but I think as a matter of protocol, if you like, that we ourselves did not volunteer to share the information without having first discussed it with Geneva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apropos Mr. Thomas Osorio, whom we mentioned at least a hundred times, do you know where he is today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You needn't answer that question. You need not say where he is. You can tell us if you know where he is.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do know where he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And he's working, is he, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: He's working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If you need to know anything else you will have to ask about it, Mr. Kovacic. You can ask the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any particular plan. I was just trying to investigate. Possibly I can find him as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, ask the Prosecution about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, during the cross-examination by my colleague, mention was made of two arrested soldiers belonging to the BH army, that apparently they were arrested by the HVO army, and that this could have been one of the factors contributing to the tension. Do you recall what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then just a very short question. Do you remember or, rather, did you hear anything in relation to this incident, that those soldiers were arrested not far, rather beyond that intersection to Travnik, which is not in the area of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: All I have to go by are my notes. You're referring to the soldiers belonging to the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The incident was explained yesterday. All I want to know is whether you're aware that it wasn't in the Vitez territory, that it was outside the territory of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: That sounds reasonable, but I don't remember exactly. I believe that the abductions took place mainly on the roads leading to and from Vitez to Zenica and Travnik, and not necessarily that the abductions took place in Vitez itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Akhavan, you did not talk to Sefkija Dzidic, the local commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Vitez, I mean, during your stay there. Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe, as I mentioned earlier, that we may have met him briefly, but that we did not have --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't really have any proper conversation? You did not talk to him?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't believe so. The only name that I have in my notes is Mehmed Alagic, who we did speak to briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the odds are against me but I still have to ask: Did you hear if those officers who had been arrested that day, that they were also released that same evening? Were you told that by anyone?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, officers of the Bosnian army who had been --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, soldiers, soldiers. I apologise. The ABiH soldiers, the ones that you mentioned who had been captured. Did anyone mention they had been released? Were you told that?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I recall, possibly at the ECMM house that was across from the British Battalion base, that they were shuttling back and forth some officials of the Bosnian army. I recall something to that effect, and it might have been part of an exchange. I vaguely recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one more question. At some point you said that the British Battalion units, rather, the British Battalion, in point of fact wasn't really competent to conduct an investigation, and you implied that it was not equipped properly for that or organised for that kind of thing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I referred to their competence, which could have been one factor, but it was more a question of what their mandate was. They had their hands quite full trying to act as peacekeepers between the two sides, regularly monitoring a very wide area with difficult terrain. So my impression is that that was not their mandate. I don't know whether they had on staff lawyers or advisors who were experts in the laws of war or humanitarian law. I don't believe that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the same time, you and Mr. Osorio, when you arrived there, you also did not have any experts along with you, people specialising in individual areas? You didn't have anyone with you. The two of you were on your own, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I had, I believe, the sufficient legal expertise. That was my role in the mission. Mr. Osorio knew the language and had considerable knowledge of the culture and peculiarities of the region, and we were assisted in military matters by members of the British Battalion who could describe to us, for example, how an attack may have taken place, what sort of weapons were used. So it was the combination of that expertise that we used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Of course. That is quite clear. Perhaps my question was not precise enough. In addition to all that knowledge that you were in position of, or Mr. Osorio, or the British Batallion, there were no other specialists, I mean, such as psychologists or forensic experts and the like?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not specifically as part of our delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, witness. Your Honours, I think I'm concluded with this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could I have a private session for literally 30 seconds and then I'll deal with my re-examination? (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you re-examine, in fact, there is one matter which I ought to raise with Mr. Kovacic, if I may. Mr. Kovacic, you haven't challenged the witness's account of the conversation with Mr. Cerkez, his conversation. Is it accepted that Mr. Cerkez, in the conversation, said he was asleep on the morning of the 16th, that there was chaos in the Vitez area, and he did not deny that the atrocities had taken place? Is it accepted that he said that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was the part which was testified on the beginning and I didn't confront it. I was just trying to add some other elements of that discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, I've got a few or quite a number of points to raise with you. First, you've been asked about your age, and your experience, and one thing and another. Getting the job with the United Nations, how did that come about? How easy was it to get that job?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was previously a member of two missions of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe, the last of which -- the first of which included among its members Ambassador Hans Corell of Sweden, who is presently the legal counsel to the Secretary-General of the United Nations. The second of which was under the leadership of the U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Commission on Human Rights. Based on that experience and based on publications and other research and expertise which I had gained in the field of international human rights law, the United Nations Centre for Human Rights hired me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they seek you out or did you seek the job?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was more by word of mouth that these sort of things would take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You speak of publications. What have you published?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: To date I have approximately 20 publications, 25 publications in various journals dealing with human rights and humanitarian law issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your formal qualifications, because we didn't bother with these, tell us what they are?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: My formal qualifications, yes. My formal qualifications is I have obtained a bachelor's of Law at Osgoode Hall law school in Toronto, a Masters of Law at Harvard law school, and I was recently appointed a visiting faculty at Yale law school in the United States.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You teach there from time to time?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another point was raised about your age and the suggestion of your involvement in this case, I think, but just tell us, within the United Nations professional band, known as the P-band, what grade do you hold?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: At present I hold a level of P-4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is one from the top, which is P-5?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what age you were when you made P-4, so that others opposite can match it to their own experience. When did you get a P-4?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Last year. So it would have been at the age of 32.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that something easy to achieve in the United Nations and regularly achieved or is that an exception? You can be immodest, because you have to be because I'm asking you the questions.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: My impression is that usually that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Typically, P-4's are people like co-counsel in the case?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Like my colleagues who are Prosecuting this case?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any case, I gather that there is no complaint or suggestion of bad faith or anything like that, so I needn't take those matters further. Let's deal with some matters of detail first. Can the witness please have Exhibit D25/1 in front of him? Perhaps it can be put on the ELMO so the point can be made clear. Do you remember this document being put to you by Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can see the context in which the question was asked, in the first paragraph in relation to Zenica's prison, you were asked about one sentence. You were asked about the third sentence down, where it says: "They are well-treated, considering the situation. About 30 showed signs of brutality." What you weren't read out was the following sentence: "After free discussions, it was learnt that they were not mistreated and those that had been harmed were so during their transportation to prison." Do you know anything about that one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. As I had mentioned earlier, we were aware that there were tensions in Zenica and we were aware that a certain number of Croats had been imprisoned, but our impression was that there was no -- I shouldn't say "no" -- but there were relatively few allegations of serious mistreatment, such as arbitrary executions or torture or the like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all with that exhibit. You were asked about fighting in a built-up area, and you were asked about that in relation to Vitez. Do you remember that question from Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly, fighting in a built-up area?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a doctrine, a military doctrine, or practice.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about something that was said by a witness called Gough. You may not remember it. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe I recall, even from my notes, having written down the initials of that military doctrine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We better see if we can find it. Which notes are these, your own handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I could be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure they are there. They may be. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe somewhere there were the initials "FBDE" or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can tell you that your answer to Mr. Sayers' question "Do you know what FIBUA style is?" was that "No, I don't." That was your answer at the time.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I did not remember what it stood for. It could be, now that you refresh my memory, that I realise what it referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, you were shown or you were read out one sentence from a statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't got the whole statement, I don't want it to be produced as an exhibit, but perhaps if this sheet can be placed on the ELMO, we can all follow it. I am afraid there's one bit of marking on it of mine, but that can be overlooked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is part of a statement of a witness called Gough, and you may remember this, Mr. Akhavan, if you look at the paragraph being shown there. I'm going to read it slowly because the interpreters, my oversight, have not been provided with a copy. "On the morning of the 16th of April, I was on patrol with the platoon commanders, call sign R10. We were in separate Warriors. We went into the Muslim area of Vitez, around the area of the racetrack, approximately at grid reference ... We could see the HVO going from house to house in FIBUA style." I pause there, Mr. Akhavan. We've been told that that is "fighting in a built-up area," and it relates to what soldiers do, may be seen to do when they are fighting in built-up areas where they might meet resistance and where they have to go into houses and confront potentially armed men.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct. I think I have in my notes some statements by British Battalion members who actually observed HVO soldiers engaged in this style of combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. Now I want you to read on to what is actually said about Vitez and see if you agree with it from your investigation.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Following after "FIBUA style"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, and I'll read it to you. "The largest group of HVO I saw was around six. They were going from house to house, clearing them of the Muslims. I only saw the odd Muslim civilian, very likely armed, offering any kind of resistance. I remember some children being moved from a window and then on to another house. All around this vicinity houses were burning and the civilians being forced out. I remember a couple of mortar rounds falling in the area of the racetrack. We were in this area for some time. The HVO were in green combat fatigues with chest-rig webbing on. I didn't see any helmets. They were wearing a coloured rag on one shoulder as a form of unit identification. I cannot remember the colour. I remember that one or two of the HVO soldiers had covered their faces with a bandanna-type piece of cloth. Some of the HVO soldiers were also dressed in black overalls. My overall impression was that the HVO were trying to clear the Muslim population from that area of the town." Now, does that passage, read in context, fit with your observations and researches or not, or do you have no comment to make?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it does fit into the descriptions which I'd received during my visits to the area, and I draw your attention to page 5 of my handwritten notes, somewhere towards the end, the fourth point being "HVO troops going house to house, shooting at BiH forces, some houses burning," and I believe somewhere else in my notes, I have something similar. But this concept of FIBUA style or going from house to house is very much what I recall being told by members of the British Battalion that I interviewed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And doing so, but with the purpose of clearing the Muslims out?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct. The impression which I gathered was that much of the fighting was with the aim of removing Muslims, mostly civilians, and that the actual resistance offered by the Bosnian army was relatively insignificant, compared to the amount of force that was used. I have in my notes also that in many cases, grenades were being thrown into homes with a view to removing civilians. I could also find those particular notes, I would need some time, but I do recall that I was told specifically that grenades were being thrown into homes where civilians were present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the suggestion is made, as it effectively has been, that the fighting in built-up areas technique to deal with resisting armed defenders explains what happened in Ahmici, that is to say, that there were armed defenders who had to be fought, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: My impression, once again, is that in Ahmici, the military presence was quite insignificant. My recollection is that this was even admitted by Colonel Blaskic in my discussions with him, once again as reflected in my notes. Those who were killed in Ahmici were overwhelmingly civilians. They included elderly, they included women, they included children. The physical destruction clearly indicated an all-encompassing attack. All livestock was killed. All homes, almost without exception, belonging to the Muslims had been burnt. In many cases, they were clearly burnt using petrol. It was clear that there was a deliberate attempt to destroy them. That, to me, indicated that this was predominantly an attack on the civilian population of the village and had very little to do with FIBUA style or any other sort of legitimate or ordinary military operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Military conclusions, insofar as you drew them from your report, were based on what?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, military conclusions were based largely on the expert advice of members of the British Battalion, on occasion, on representatives of the ECMM, but I believe that the military analysis of the situation was only tangentially relevant to us in the preparation of our reports. Whether the Muslims had provoked the hostilities or whether the Croats had provoked the hostilities was quite irrelevant to the focus of our investigation, which was violations of humanitarian law. All sorts of tricks and strategies and tactics were used between the two sides in their conflicts with one another, but the fact remains that we had in Ahmici and in other areas attacks which demonstrated clearly an attempt to eradicate virtually the entire civilian population, and that, to us, was the essential focus of our mandate, to investigate human rights abuses, violations of humanitarian law. The military context often would help us understand how a situation may have escalated to the point where civilians were slaughtered, where civilian property was destroyed, but strictly speaking, we were not there as military experts, we were not there as part of a peacekeeping mission, we were not there as intelligence officers to try and make sophisticated analyses of the military situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bodies piled up opposite the cemetery has been raised as a topic. What's the totality but in absolute summary, a couple of sentences, of what you knew from sources about that?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In that particular location, across from the Catholic cemetery, what I knew was that the British Battalion had recovered approximately 20 bodies. The bodies were mainly, if not exclusively, that of people in civilian clothes, including women, elderly, children. Many had been shot in the head or the neck, according to the members of the British Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were they piled up or lined up opposite the cemetery, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It could have been on the afternoon of the 16th of April, but most probably a day or two after --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: -- when it was safe enough for the British Battalion to collect the bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The truck bomb, in a sentence, what was your view on that? Because you may not have written about it in detail.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The truck bomb is reflected in my handwritten notes, as well as the report which we eventually submitted to the Human Rights Commission. It was very clear, from seeing that region of Vitez, that there was a massive explosion involving extensive damage. We were told that the truck was filled with explosives and that a local Muslim was handcuffed to the steering wheel of the truck and the truck was forced into that region of the city, where it was detonated. What we did see clearly is that there had been a massive explosion. Since it was not a war in which there were aerial bombardment or other means of delivering that sort of explosion, the explanation seemed credible enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The list of 18 names, is it available now and, if so, by what means?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe it should be in the files of the Commission of Experts established by the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the only place where it's to be found?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, I'm not sure whether it has found its way into the investigative files of the Prosecutor's office. This, I'm not sure about, since I've not been involved in the investigation --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you had any involvement in this case?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the present case?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've not been involved in any investigative matters. My only involvement was in the Blaskic case on two purely abstract, legal questions, one involving the mens rea of command responsibility, the other involving the powers of the Tribunal to issue binding orders to the Republic of Croatia, but nothing related to the specific facts of the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've put to you that part of the Blaskic defence, that is, part of Blaskic's evidence, is correct in relation to matters of which you give evidence, and therefore I want to ask you this, and it may be that the break comes -- if it does come -- comes at a potentially convenient time: Were you aware at the time of your investigation of any other investigation being made and, in particular, of any investigation being made by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. We were not aware of any such investigations, and I assume that Messrs. Kordic, Blaskic, Cerkez had every opportunity to inform us during the meeting whether there was such an investigation, and, indeed, we would have been very happy to hear from them that they were taking this matter seriously, nor are we aware of any investigations which took place subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the name "Anto Sliskovic" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a few more questions of this witness, but only a few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be convenient if you can finish, or do you want some time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What I was going to propose was -- because I don't propose to produce as an exhibit a document of which I can say nothing, save that it was produced in another case -- but it may be that if we were to take a break and Mr. Akhavan was able to have an opportunity to read an unmarked copy of that document, then I could ask him for some comments on particular passages of it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. Half past eleven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, you've now read the document that was handed to you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a few questions to ask about specific passages, but just tell me first, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard of its existence before?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any comments that you want to make in relation to the covering letter from a man called Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The covering letter --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you do, I'll place the -- or I'll have the usher place a copy of that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are, of course, copies available to the Court but I make it plain, I don't want to produce it as an exhibit for obvious reasons. So if the Court would prefer to have copies to handle, then they can be made available on whatever basis they like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's start by putting it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm wondering, first of all, whether this is indeed the same document that was shown to me by the Defence. I recall a similar document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, this hasn't been shown to you by the Defence. This is an entirely different document, produced in another case, but I simply want your comments on it. The first sheet is the covering letter --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- with the date 25th of May, 1993, headed, "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatian Community, Croatian Defence Council," signed or typed at the bottom "Sliskovic", but the original is signed. What comment do you have to make about this?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have a couple of comments. First of all, I find it surprising that this document is a military secret that is strictly confidential. Nothing contained in this document would appear to me to be a military secret of any sort and, if anything, I think that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna could have gained considerable propaganda value from making this document public and it surprises me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The secret passage is cut off from -- could you move the document down a bit, please? Move it down a bit or up. Yes. Anything else on the covering letter?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The other -- where it says that: "It was impossible to obtain statements of the persons of Muslim nationality who have fled to the areas of Zenica and Travnik," that may be true but there were a significant number of Muslims who were actually being detained by the HVO in various places under their control. So I think it is incredulous to say that they did not have access to statements of the persons of Muslim nationality. Those would be two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Second sheet, please. I have some questions on this but you may first of all have your own comments. I don't know if you do.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not specifically with respect to this page, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, therefore, turn your attention to the bottom of the page, if the usher would be so good? Thank you very much. The paragraphs beginning: "However, the ABiH leadership, especially the leadership of the 3rd Corps and its more extreme part, the 7th Muslim Brigade, kept on insisting on its thesis of taking full control of these areas. This time, they resorted to more subtle methods. Among other things, they brought in the extreme part of the refugee population from the areas of Jajce, Kotor Varos, Kljuc, Prijedor and other towns, thus achieving the effect of outnumbering the rest of the population, causing there ..." Did you have evidence to support, match, or counter that, or was it outside the area of your inquiry?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We did know there were a number of Muslim refugees from other parts of Bosnia, some of whom had come to stay with friends or relatives in Ahmici, and we were told that the Bosnian Croat leadership was concerned that this influx of Muslim refugees would upset the ethnic balance and, of course, this occurred in the context of the Vance-Owen Plan demarcating this canton as a Croat canton. So demographics was always a very sensitive issue. But this idea that the 7th Muslim Brigade had deliberately selected extremist refugees, I find that hard to believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any evidence of that yourself?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: None whatsoever. I don't even know how one selects extremist refugees. People either are refugees or they're not. When you have several hundred men, women, children, families as refugees, I don't know how one could characterise them as extremists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apparently I misread the passage and left out the word "Muslim" before "refugee". Can it be noted? The next sentence reads --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Excuse me, Mr. Nice. I should like to know what is the origin of this document, because you're showing us documents without introducing them. We can't work like that. We have to know where that document comes from. You must introduce the document to the Chamber so that they can follow. Will you tell us where it comes from? What is its origin? When was it produced? Could you please first inform us before putting questions to the witness about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I explained it yesterday, and it is essential that this matter can be dealt with because of the conduct of the Defence. The Defence are plainly adopting Blaskic. It may well that they're going to be calling Blaskic, because they could hardly be adopting his evidence to put it to a witness unless they had seen him, proofed him, and had that in mind as a possibility. There would be no other grounds for their preferring his evidence over someone else's. This document was introduced, as I explained yesterday, at a late stage, without a witness producing it in the Blaskic case. It is the only other known alleged contemporaneous report relating to Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We ask Mr. Nice to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- that if the Defence were to rely on this document, then they should have put its contents to this witness. Indeed Judge Robinson, I think via the Presiding Judge, made the point that I could deal with it in re-examination. Because the Defence hadn't put it, and because it may very well arise as something to be dealt with in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Nice slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well, but regarding this document, we can see on the ELMO the first part of the document. What is this document? It doesn't matter what the Defence has done, but the Trial Chamber has to know what this document is. It was produced in Blaskic, but what is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The document in the Blaskic defence, which introduced it, is said to be a report prepared by Sliskovic in May 1993 on the Ahmici events, and it has the covering letter, and I think in the English translation three sheets, in the original it is, of course, in the Croatian language, and again with a covering letter and three sheets. It was introduced in Blaskic. I'm not sure how it was introduced. I think without any witness it was placed in as a document and is no doubt being considered by the Chamber in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) But we see "military secret", but what army is it? I'm still not satisfied by this manner of presenting documents. I'm sorry. I don't think you can do it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let us try and resolve the position in this way: This is not a document on which you rely. What would you say about it in argument? Is it a truthful document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the moment, the document, having come relatively recently into the possession of this team of Prosecutors, as indeed into the team of those prosecuting in Blaskic, is a document that cries out for further inquiries, maybe inquiries of the state concerned, but at this stage, my duty is to forecast what may be raised and what reasonably may be raised by way of Defence arguments that should have been and could be put to this witness, and to ask his comments on them. The Chamber is particularly assisted in this way of dealing with things, because Mr. Akhavan, who is, of course, an -- he is not an expert, in one sense, but he's very nearly an expert, he's an on-the-ground investigator and the only one, apart from his colleague, of whom we know, and the Chamber has the opportunity of seeing him come fresh to this document and give his observations on certain passages of it. This, I think, was forecast by your colleague, Judge Robinson, yesterday as the appropriate way of dealing with the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we're getting the cart before the horse. This is the problem. We haven't got the document in. Somebody is being asked to comment on it. Perhaps it may be simpler if we deal with the matter in this way, and I turn to the Defence: Is anybody going to rely on this document before we go into it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The answer is no, from our side, from the Kordic perspective.
