Indeed, although Mr. Nice has done a nice job of setting up something so he can use the back door to get something else in and use this witness to comment, the truth is we asked this witness, relative to the Kordic interview -- strike that -- relative to the Blaskic interview only and using Blaskic's testimony in that regard, that's all. We don't accept the entire Blaskic case. It's not ours. That's just something Mr. Nice suggests or made up. That's not our position. We didn't accept the entire case. We don't have the evidence. We don't have the documents from Blaskic. That's one of the issues we want to raise at the Status Conference. Moreover, and last but not least, while I'm on my feet, the issues being raised in terms of what responsibility was done for investigations is covered by the witness's own notes at page 34, where in his interview with Mr. Kordic, Mr. Kordic announces that there was an investigation formed. It's right there for the Court to see in one of the exhibits. I don't know what we're doing at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, our position is slightly different, and, of course, that must be clear from the proceedings so far, because my client was a commander of a brigade, which we admit from the beginning, and he was subordinate to Blaskic; therefore, that document is of interest to us. However, we have not shown this document to the witness, nor have we questioned him about it, because it is a document that was issued after his inquiries. Yesterday, my learned friend, the Prosecutor, told us after the hearing that he had that document, and you must have noticed that I reacted immediately with interest, wanting to see that document, but for another reason. Colleague Nice said that this was a document dated the 25th of May which the Blaskic Defence had introduced as an exhibit quite recently, that is, at the very end of the trial of Blaskic. I know that an exhibit was, indeed, introduced in the Blaskic case towards the end of the proceedings, that is, related to the investigation, but that document, according to the information that I received from colleagues in that case, that document, I was told that the document was under seal, and that is why I could not get it. When the Prosecutor said that he had a document related to the investigation introduced recently, of course, I immediately thought that that might be that document. However, the document that we received after the hearing yesterday and which has been produced now and is marked from the Blaskic case, D608, was at the time, though I cannot assert that with certainty, two documents were introduced regarding the investigation, because apparently Blaskic did receive some reports about the investigation. I knew that that existed, though I never saw that document, because this technical side of disclosure of documents, in accordance with your previous order and the assistance of the Registry, takes time, and according to the latest information that we have from the Registry, we will get that document from the Blaskic case, probably before the autumn session. We have already received many of the documents from the first part of the trial. But what is important is the following: My learned friend Nice is now producing this document, and he wants to ask the witness about that document, based on the assumption that the Defence will be putting questions regarding that document. When? We have finished with our cross-examination of the witness and we did not produce that document. So I think that it is not proper for him to discuss that document now in the redirect. Whether we will be questioning other witnesses about it, when and how, I don't know. We'll see. That is all I wish to say as my contribution to clearing up the situation before you make your ruling, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two points: I'm surprised that what should be -- that those representing Kordic should say that they are as selective as they are about Blaskic's evidence, for if they have no intention of calling or adopting his case, by implication saying they are only accepting that bits of it are true, how can they be putting positively -- as they did when invited by Your Honour -- how can they be putting positively that something is true, and it was put vigorously to this witness, when they aren't even adopting the provider of that material as a potential witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with that in due course. Let's look at this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second point is that this document may well prove to be a document we will produce, because if it's a document that is manifestly a dishonest document, then there would be relevance for this Chamber in this body producing, whenever it may have done, a dishonest document. Of course, we've only had it recently, and inquiries that may have to be carried out further to investigate its status and history have yet to be performed, but at this stage, it would be valuable in the extreme to have, from this witness, untutored, completely spontaneous reaction to its comments. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we think the better way to deal with this is to see what, if any, use is made from this document. If any use is made of it, then we shall give leave for this witness to be recalled to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps the document could come off the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn to your notes at page 29, please?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The page beginning with "Vitez Brigade"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. The fourth line down from there, where Blaskic is recorded as accepting responsibility for the area with no military operations without his commands, did he make any exception to that? Did he qualify that in any way, identifying troops that were not under his command?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your notes, page 35. Still with Blaskic, can you just explain that entry there that relates to Blaskic? Because it's out of sequence.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I did not meet with Colonel Blaskic a second time. I don't know if this is something which someone else told me about Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't have a recollection of it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following entry, which says that the priest had reason to believe something, did the priest give you his reasons?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall whether I actually met the priest or whether this was the recollection of the padre of the British Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question relates to Cerkez. You told us something, when you were answering questions initially, about his reaction to your inquiries, "nervousness," I think, was the word you used. You told Mr. Kovacic more about his change of demeanour when Stewart arrived, but when you were speaking of his general disposition, to what part of the encounter were you speaking?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was speaking to when Colonel Stewart entered the room. I think it was clear that Mr. Cerkez paid considerable deference to Colonel Stewart, not necessarily the sort of respect which comes out of personal liking, but perhaps more out of respect for authority. When Colonel Stewart began to explain that this investigation on the part of the U.N. Human Rights Commission represented, and his words, as I recall were, "the conscience of the International Community" and that Mario Cerkez would be held liable for investigating this matter to the extent that his subordinates were involved and to take effective action against any perpetrators, I think at that point, he became visibly nervous and uneasy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Cerkez, at any time, identify any local units that were not under his control?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that both Colonel Blaskic and Cerkez did refer to HOS, but I believe that certainly Mr. Blaskic, possibly to a lesser extent Mr. Cerkez, suggested that they are in control of the region. Mr. Cerkez suggested that on the day of the attack, there was some sort of chaos, that there was a sort of spontaneous resistance to a Muslim offensive. I don't know whether I would interpret that to suggest that the HVO was not in control of the region. But I'm just going to double check by consulting my notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 29 -- I beg your pardon --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's page 32 and 33, my meeting with Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: He says that HOS was present, it was mixed Muslim and Croat, and there was no HOS in Vitez, that they came from Zenica. So my interpretation of that would be that HOS was in the region, though it was not from the region, and that there was chaos on the day of the attack, not so much because there were external elements but because, according to Mr. Cerkez, the Bosnian Croats were taken by surprise. But I don't think anyone suggested that HOS was in any significant control in the region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. HOS apart, was Cerkez identifying any local brigades or subbrigades that were not under local authority?
